turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, I came in because of work, mostly. I'm a cashier, and lately at the register I just keep getting stuck doing things that... that don't really fit the moment. Like, I'll start tapping the scanner in this specific pattern. They just installed these new handheld scanners, actually, the ones with the red rubber grips? They're supposed to be ergonomic, but my manager didn't even train us on them. He just left them at the lanes. I have a bachelor's degree, you know, I shouldn't even be dealing with this, but the job market is just... anyway, I'll be tapping the scanner, or I'll just completely freeze up with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer. Just stuck there, not moving, while the customer is waiting. This one guy was buying windshield wiper fluid and he just stared at me. I always buy the blue fluid, not the orange, the orange leaves a weird film on the glass if it dries too fast in the sun. But yeah, he complained, and last week my manager actually wrote me up for it, so... that's why I'm here.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, frequently drifting off-topic to discuss scanner ergonomics, their degree, and windshield wiper fluid preferences.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes severe motor disturbances, including freezing in place (catalepsy/posturing) and repetitively tapping the scanner (stereotypy) inappropriately while working.

turns.doctor_question: When you perform that tapping pattern at the register, do you feel like you have to do it to prevent something bad from happening or to relieve a sense of internal tension?
turns.patient_response: No, it's not like that. I don't feel like I have to do it, it's just... I just do it. Like I'm not trying to stop anything bad. Bad things happen anyway, you know? Like my car, the transmission went out last month, and I didn't see that coming at all. I was just driving down 4th street, right by that old diner they closed down—shame, they had really good cherry pie, the kind with the thick crust—and boom, it just stopped shifting. Had to get a tow. The tow truck driver was this guy who wouldn't stop talking about his fantasy football team. I mean, I don't even watch football, I prefer baseball. The pacing is better. But anyway, no, I don't feel any tension or anything before I tap the scanner. It just happens.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, wandering off-topic to discuss a broken car, a closed diner, cherry pie, and fantasy football before returning to the original point.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies performing the tapping behavior to prevent something bad from happening or to relieve internal tension.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any problems with your memory or your ability to think clearly lately, perhaps things like forgetting recent conversations or having trouble following complex instructions?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't think so. My memory is fine. I actually have a really good memory for conversations. Like, just yesterday my neighbor was talking to me about his gutters. He was up on a ladder—one of those aluminum extension ones? You have to be careful with those, the locking mechanism can slip if you don't set it right. My cousin broke his collarbone falling off a ladder back in '98. He had to wear this brace that kept his shoulders pulled all the way back, he looked like he was standing at attention for the military. He never even served, though. He wanted to get into the Navy, but he had flat feet. I don't know why flat feet matter on a boat, honestly, you're just walking on steel decks anyway. Steel gets so hot in the sun, you could probably fry an egg on it. I like my eggs over easy, usually, with some dark rye toast. But yeah, no, my thinking is completely clear. I haven't forgotten anything.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from gutters to ladders, a cousin's injury, the Navy, flat feet, steel decks, and finally frying eggs.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient explicitly denies having any problems with memory or clear thinking, stating their memory is fine and thinking is completely clear.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear sounds or voices that other people around you cannot hear?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, I guess so. Most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me. Sometimes they're calling my name from the stockroom, or saying I rang something up wrong. Ringing things up can be tricky with the produce codes, honestly. The stickers on the organic avocados are so tiny now. Avocados go bad so fast, too—you buy them hard as a rock and then two days later they're just brown mush. I tried making guacamole last year, but I put way too much lime juice in it. Lime juice is really good in iced tea, though, especially in the summer. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll hear them talking or telling me I messed up the transaction, but when I turn around, there’s nobody there. Just empty space. And the customers never react, so I know no one else heard it. I don't know how the baggers would hear anything anyway, half of them wear those little wireless earbuds on shift, which is definitely against company policy. The employee handbook specifically says no personal electronics on the floor. It's printed in this really tiny font, like size eight or something, on that cheap paper that tears if you turn the page too fast... but yeah, nobody else hears the people talking.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient confirms hearing voices of people talking or calling their name when no one is there and others do not hear them.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits significant tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the topic of hearing voices to avocado stickers, guacamole, lime juice, and the font size of the employee handbook.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever been told by a doctor that you have a medical condition, such as a head injury, seizure disorder, or any other physical illness that might be affecting your brain?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't. No doctor's ever told me anything like that. I mean, I've never had a seizure or a real head injury. I did bump my head on the kitchen cabinet a few weeks ago because I left the door open while I was unloading the dishwasher, but it didn't even leave a bruise. Those cabinets are so old anyway, they're made of that cheap particle board where the fake wood veneer starts peeling off at the corners if it gets too humid. 

And it gets incredibly humid in my apartment during the summer. I bought this little window AC unit from a garage sale a couple of years ago, but the filter is always getting clogged with dust. Dust is a huge problem in my building. The vents are all connected, so if the guy downstairs burns his toast, my whole place smells like smoke for hours. He's always burning things, I think he falls asleep with the oven on or something. You really shouldn't do that, it's a massive fire hazard. They actually make you watch a whole safety video about fire hazards when you get hired at the grocery store. It's on this ancient VHS tape that skips right in the middle, right when the cartoon fire extinguisher is talking. 

But yeah, no, my brain is fine, physically. I haven't been diagnosed with any medical conditions like that.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from bumping their head to cabinets, humidity, AC units, dust, a neighbor's cooking, and a grocery store safety video before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been hearing these voices?
turns.patient_response:
Well, the voices and, you know, the moments where things just seem really out of place... that's been going on for about three months now. Give or take. It started right around the time they changed the layout of the cereal aisle at work. They moved all the oatmeal to the bottom shelf, which makes zero sense because oatmeal is a staple. People buy it all the time, especially the instant packets with the little dinosaur eggs that melt when you add hot water. I used to love those when I was a kid. My mom would always make it for me before school, but she'd use milk instead of water so it was creamier. 

Milk is getting so expensive lately, though. A gallon of whole milk is almost five dollars at my store, even with the employee discount. The discount isn't even that great, honestly, it's only ten percent and it doesn't apply to sale items. And everything is always on sale with those bright yellow tags. The ink on those tags smudges if your fingers are even a little bit sweaty, and then you get black ink all over your hands. It takes forever to wash off, even if you use that gritty orange soap they keep in the mechanics' bathrooms. 

But yeah, about three months. That's when I really started noticing them talking when no one was there.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient confirms hearing voices talking when no one is there.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech is highly tangential, drifting from the topic of voices to cereal aisles, oatmeal, childhood memories, milk prices, and hand soap before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the voices you hear, do you have any firm beliefs about things happening around you—such as people tracking you, or secret messages being sent to you—that others seem to disagree with?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I mean, nobody's tracking me or sending me secret messages or anything like that. I just go to work and come home, mostly. Although, speaking of tracking, they did just install these new security cameras above the self-checkout lanes last week. They look like those little black domes, you know? Like half a magic 8-ball stuck to the ceiling. I always wondered how those magic 8-balls worked when I was little. I cracked one open once in my parents' driveway with a hammer, and it was just this dark blue liquid that smelled terrible. It stained the concrete for years. My dad was so mad about that stain. He used to try to pressure wash it every spring, but it never fully came out. Pressure washers are incredibly loud, too. You have to wear ear protection if you're going to use one for more than a few minutes, otherwise your ears ring for the rest of the day. But no, no secret messages or anything like that. Just the voices sometimes.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having firm beliefs about being tracked or receiving secret messages.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient confirms experiencing auditory hallucinations by stating they hear 'just the voices sometimes.'
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from security cameras to magic 8-balls, a driveway stain, and pressure washers.

turns.doctor_question: When you are speaking, do you feel like your thoughts are sometimes racing, or that you have difficulty keeping your train of thought on track?
turns.patient_response: Well, I don't really feel like they're racing, exactly. Sometimes I just have a lot to say, or I think of something else while I'm talking. Like right now, I'm thinking about how I need to organize my closet. It's a disaster in there. I have all these old sweaters from college that I never wear anymore, but I can't bring myself to throw them away. They're mostly wool, and wool is so itchy, you know? I don't know how people used to wear wool all the time before they invented synthetic fabrics. Polyester is much softer, even if it doesn't breathe as well. If you wear polyester in the summer, you just sweat right through it. And then you have to do laundry, which is a whole other chore. The coin machine at the laundromat down the street is always broken. It just eats your quarters and doesn't give you any change. Quarters are getting hard to find anyway, nobody uses cash anymore. Everyone just taps their phones at the register. It makes my job easier, I guess, but I kind of miss the sound of the cash drawer popping open. It had a nice little bell sound. Ding! Just like that. But yeah, no, my thoughts don't really race, I just have a lot of them.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting continuously from organizing a closet to sweaters, wool, polyester, laundry, quarters, and cash registers.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient explicitly denies experiencing racing thoughts, stating 'I don't really feel like they're racing' and 'my thoughts don't really race'.

turns.doctor_question: Have you found yourself losing interest in activities you used to enjoy, or feeling like you have very little energy or motivation to do things lately?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I don't know about energy, exactly, but... I mean, I still care about my wife and kids, of course I do. But lately I just don't seem to have the push to call my son at college. He's at the state university, studying business or something. I always thought business degrees were a little vague, you know? Like, what do you actually learn to do? It's not like learning a trade. Plumbers make fantastic money these days. My neighbor had a plumber out last month to fix a leaky pipe under his sink, and the guy charged him two hundred dollars just to show up. Just to pull into the driveway! His truck was really nice, though. One of those big F-250s with the dual rear wheels. You really only need those if you're towing something heavy, like a big fifth-wheel camper. My wife and I used to talk about getting an RV and driving cross-country, maybe seeing the Grand Canyon. I've heard the Grand Canyon is smaller in person than you'd expect, but the colors are supposed to be beautiful at sunset. 

But anyway, yeah, I just don't have the motivation. I haven't been meeting up with my kayak group either, or even working on my little repair projects in the garage. And when people ask what's wrong, I mostly just shrug because I can't really find much to say about it.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from his son's college to plumbers, trucks, and the Grand Canyon before returning to the original topic.
symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient describes a lack of motivation (avolition) and having little to say when asked what is wrong (alogia).
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly states he has lost motivation and stopped participating in previously enjoyed activities like his kayak group and repair projects.

turns.doctor_question: During these past three months, have there been any periods where you felt so down, hopeless, or empty that it was hard to get through the day, even when you weren't hearing the voices?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't think so. I haven't really felt sad or hopeless, or... empty. Well, the only thing empty right now is the windshield washer fluid reservoir in my Honda. I keep meaning to grab a jug of it from the auto aisle at work, but I always forget by the end of my shift. You really have to make sure you get the kind with antifreeze in it during the winter, the orange stuff, not the blue stuff. I made the mistake of just using water once when I ran out, and the whole line froze solid overnight. The mechanic had to thaw the entire system out with a heat gun. 

Heat guns are incredibly useful tools, actually. You can use them for stripping paint, too. My wife wanted to refinish this old antique dresser we found at a garage sale a few years back, and we used a heat gun to get all the old varnish off. It smells awful, though. Melting varnish has this really sharp, chemical smell that just gets stuck in your nose for days. You definitely have to do it outside or in a well-ventilated area, otherwise you'll get a terrible headache. I think we ended up painting it a sort of seafoam green, which was really popular for a while. But yeah, I don't feel down or anything like that. Just kind of regular, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the concept of feeling empty to windshield washer fluid, heat guns, and refinishing furniture.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling sad or empty.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient explicitly denies feeling hopeless.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned the voices and the other experiences have been happening for about three months; have you ever had any similar experiences, even briefly, before that three-month period?
turns.patient_response: No, not before that. It's just been these last three months. I mean, three months feels like a long time, though, doesn't it? Like, a whole season. Winter is almost three months long, and by the end of it, you're just so tired of the snow. Shoveling the driveway is the worst part. My shovel has this ergonomic handle, it's supposed to save your back, but honestly, I think it just makes it harder to lift the heavy, wet snow. You know the kind I mean? The stuff the plow leaves right at the end of the driveway. It's like wet cement. My neighbor bought a snowblower last year, a two-stage one with an electric start. He clears his driveway in ten minutes flat. I keep thinking I should get one, but they take up so much room in the garage. And then you have to deal with the gas and oil, and making sure the carburetor doesn't get gummed up over the summer. Small engines are so finicky. If you don't use a fuel stabilizer, the ethanol in the gas just ruins everything. I had a lawnmower that wouldn't start for three weeks because of bad gas. I ended up having to take it to this little repair shop on the edge of town. The guy who runs it is a character, always wearing these grease-stained overalls. But yeah, no, nothing like this before three months ago.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a very long, verbose response to a simple yes/no question, talking extensively about unrelated topics.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from the duration of their symptoms to winter, snow shovels, snowblowers, small engines, and a repair shop before finally returning to the point.
